ARTICLE

Financing Compute: The $1.8 Trillion Bet on AI Data Centers

Data Centers

November 19, 2026

Key Takeaways:

$794 billion: Capital raised by data center developers between 3Q 2025 and 1H 2026
56%: Share of colocation financing from private markets in 1H 2026
18x: The year-over-year increase in neocloud maturing debt between 2029 and 2030

Executive summary

Players driving the global data center buildout have raised around $1.8 trillion in financing since 2020, and capital expenditures are surging alongside demand for artificial intelligence. Firms have tapped new capital sources and deal structures while markets are pricing in higher credit risks, creating refinancing pressure for at least $1 trillion of debt maturing within the next five years.

Volume: Companies developing data centers raised at least $1.8 trillion between 2020 and the first half of 2026 across debt, equity and securitized instruments. Nearly half of that total was raised between 3Q 2025 and 1H 2026, with private markets playing a growing role. Financing for the large group of colocation providers exceeds that of the four hyperscalers.
Refinancing: Rising interest rates, growing concerns around developers’ debt levels and an overreliance on financing support from hyperscalers and chipmakers are placing greater refinancing pressure on firms. Colocation providers and neoclouds, in particular, face steep increases in maturing debt volumes by 2030, with smaller developers like TeraWulf and Crusoe facing higher uncertainties due to large amounts of construction debt. Execution challenges have already affected Firmus and Nscale’s high-valuation IPO plans.
Structure: Deal structures are becoming more complex, leveraging credit support mechanisms from investment-grade backers to enable smaller developers to raise capital at the size and tenor required. Support mechanisms include GPU-backed loans, direct guarantees, residual-value guarantees and prepayments. Nvidia has extended at least $198 billion in direct credit support, committing even more alongside large asset managers.
Banks: Morgan Stanley underwrote the most data center financing, driven in part by its close relationship with Meta. Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase follow. TD Bank and Scotiabank accelerated dealmaking the most in 2026, competing to fund established players.
Approach: BNEF compiled over 2,000 transactions of the largest 125 data center developers across Bloomberg Terminal, third party and news sources, and collected additional sector- and deal-level details through industry interviews and document reviews.
